title: What Does It Actually Mean to Get Better at a Subject? Eight research-informed principles for designing curriculum progression
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: Sarah Findlater, writing up her researchED Doha session, asks what it really means for a pupil to get better at a subject, a question curriculum documents often assume rather than answer. She distils a summer of reading on expertise, knowledge, disciplinary thinking, sequencing and assessment into eight research-informed principles for designing curriculum progression. Each principle pairs a big idea with a named source (Counsell, Willingham, Myatt, Chi and colleagues, Goldman, Soderstrom and Bjork, the National Research Council, Christodoulou, Harris and colleagues) and a practical question for curriculum designers. She is explicit that these are her interpretation rather than a tested framework. Her department is now applying them in English across Key Stage 3, starting from what pupils should understand more deeply rather than from the units already taught. The central shift is to treat progression as a developing relationship between knowledge, understanding and disciplinary thinking instead of a ladder of harder content.
points: Progression needs a subject-specific definition of improvement, so generic verbs like analyse or evaluate are not enough to say what a more accomplished pupil can do.
Repeating content is not progression; each return to a concept should demand or reveal something new, and the curriculum should say what that is.
Success in a lesson is not durable learning, so progression models should plan retrieval and application after time has passed, with less support.
Assessment tasks should be designed to reveal the understanding you want, and broad progression statements should guide teaching rather than label pupils.
Findlater's English department begins from what pupils should understand by the end of a key stage, then works back to the knowledge and concepts that must be secure first.
quotes: But I started wondering whether we always have a sufficiently clear picture of what we mean by getting better. Does progression mean knowing more? Remembering more?
Identify what pupils should know, understand and do increasingly well. Look beyond generic skills such as analyse or evaluate. Describe what improvement looks like within the subject itself.
The big idea: Repeating content is not the same as progressing. The research: Mary Myatt (2022) argues for connecting curriculum content through important concepts that develop over time.
The big idea: Success today doesn’t necessarily mean learning that lasts. The research: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015) distinguish immediate performance from durable learning.
The big idea: Assessment should reveal learning, not simply produce a score. The research: The National Research Council (2001) connects learning, assessment tasks and interpretation of evidence.

The big idea: A progression model should inform teaching, not simply categorise pupils. The research: Harris, Adie and Wyatt-Smith (2022) found support for formative uses of progression-based assessment, with more limited evidence for summative and accountability purposes.

Rather than beginning with the units we teach and trying to fit progression statements around them, we are beginning to ask some different questions. What should pupils understand more deeply by the end of a key stage?

The biggest shift in my thinking this summer has been moving away from viewing progression as a sequence of increasingly difficult content and towards seeing it as a developing relationship between knowledge, understanding and disciplinary thinking. That doesn’t make curriculum design simpler.
context: Curriculum documents often assume a shared meaning of improvement that nobody has stated.
Subject-specific descriptions of improvement replace vague skill verbs.
Revisiting a concept only counts as progress if each encounter adds something new.
Lesson success can mask learning that will not last, so retrieval has to come later.
Assessment tasks must be built to show the understanding the curriculum aims for.
Progression models earn their place by guiding teaching, not by labelling pupils.
Starting from end-of-key-stage understanding reverses the usual unit-first planning.
Progression is reframed as knowledge, understanding and thinking developing together.
